note.specFocus: Key beliefs: the divine presence (Shekhinah). How God's presence was experienced in the Tenakh (the Tabernacle and the Temple) and how Jews understand and experience it today.
note.summary:
The Shekhinah: God's presence on earth
"Shekhinah" comes from the Hebrew root sh-kh-n, "to dwell" or "to settle". It means the presence of God dwelling among people. The word does not appear in the Tenakh but is used by the rabbis in the Talmud and Midrash. It describes how a God who is beyond the universe (transcendent) can also be close to people (immanent).

In the Tenakh
• In the wilderness God told Moses, "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8). The word for dwell, v'shakhanti, shares the Shekhinah root.
• When the Tabernacle (Mishkan) was finished, "the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). God's presence was also shown as a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21).
• When Solomon dedicated the First Temple in Jerusalem, a cloud filled the house and the priests could not stand to serve (1 Kings 8:10–11). The innermost room, the Holy of Holies, was thought of as the special place of God's presence. Only the High Priest entered it, once a year on Yom Kippur.
• The prophets describe God's glory filling the Temple (Isaiah 6:1–3, "the whole earth is full of his glory").

After the Temple
• The Second Temple was destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE. The rabbis taught that the Shekhinah did not abandon Israel but went into exile with the people (Talmud, Megillah 29a).
• The Shekhinah is found wherever Jews pray and study: "If ten sit together and occupy themselves with Torah, the Shekhinah rests among them", and even two (Pirkei Avot 3:2 and 3:6). This helps explain why a minyan (ten adults) is needed for communal prayer.
• The Shekhinah is linked to acts of kindness. The Talmud teaches that God visits the sick, so Jews should do the same (Sotah 14a).
• Some traditions link the Shekhinah with Shabbat. In Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) the Shekhinah is the feminine aspect of God, and the Kabbalat Shabbat song Lecha Dodi welcomes the Sabbath "bride".

Diversity of views
• Orthodox Jews pray three times daily for the rebuilding of the Temple and the return of the Shekhinah to Zion. The Amidah includes the words "who restores his Shekhinah to Zion".
• Many Reform and Liberal Jews do not pray for the Temple to be rebuilt. They understand the Shekhinah more as an experience of God's closeness in community, ethical action and nature.
• Many Jews feel God's presence at the Western Wall (Kotel), the last remaining part of the Temple complex, where people place written prayers in the cracks.

Why it matters
Belief in the Shekhinah reassures Jews that God is close and cares, even in suffering and exile. It gives meaning to communal worship, study and kindness, and it explains the importance of Jerusalem and the Temple Mount.

Key terms: Shekhinah; Mishkan (Tabernacle); Holy of Holies; immanence; transcendence; minyan; Kotel.

questions.question:
What is the meaning of the Hebrew term Shekhinah?
A The written law
B The divine presence of God
C The coming of the Messiah
D The world to come
questions.modelAnswer: B – the divine presence. Shekhinah comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to dwell" and refers to God's presence among people. The written law is the Torah or Tenakh, the Messiah is the Mashiach, and the world to come is Olam Ha-Ba.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Write only the letter of the answer you choose; one mark is for the correct term or fact.

questions.question:
Which one of the following places was believed to be the special dwelling place of God's presence in the Temple?
A The bimah
B The women's gallery
C The Holy of Holies
D The outer courtyard
questions.modelAnswer: C – the Holy of Holies, the innermost room of the Temple. Only the High Priest entered it, once a year on Yom Kippur. The bimah is a synagogue reading platform.
evidence: Leviticus 16 (High Priest on the Day of Atonement)

questions.question: Give two ways in which the Shekhinah is described in the Tenakh.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two from:
• As a cloud that filled the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34).
• As a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night leading the Israelites.
• As God's glory filling Solomon's Temple.
• As God dwelling in the sanctuary among the people (Exodus 25:8).
• As fire on Mount Sinai.
questions.examTip: Give two separate, accurate points; short phrases are enough. Do not spend time explaining, and do not repeat the same idea in different words.

questions.question: Give two ways in which Jews today may experience the Shekhinah.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any two from:
• Praying together in a minyan.
• Studying Torah with others.
• Praying at the Western Wall in Jerusalem.
• Welcoming Shabbat.
• Doing acts of kindness such as visiting the sick.
• Private prayer and meditation.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the Shekhinah influences Jews today.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It encourages communal prayer and study. The rabbis taught that when ten people gather to study Torah, the Shekhinah rests among them. Many Jews therefore attend synagogue to pray with a minyan, or join study groups (chavruta), believing that God is especially present when the community meets.

2. It gives special importance to Jerusalem and the Western Wall. The Shekhinah was believed to dwell in the Holy of Holies of the Temple. Jews face Jerusalem when they pray the Amidah, and many visit the Kotel to pray and leave notes in its cracks, feeling close to God where the Temple once stood. Orthodox Jews also pray for the Shekhinah's return to Zion.
evidence: Amidah: "who restores his Shekhinah to Zion"
questions.examTip: Make two distinct points. Develop each one (a simple point earns 1 mark, a detailed one 2 marks) by saying how or why it shapes what Jews believe or do today. If the question asks for contrasting ways, make sure the two are genuinely different, for example Orthodox and Reform.

questions.question: Explain two contrasting Jewish understandings of the Shekhinah today.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Many Orthodox Jews link the Shekhinah closely to the Temple in Jerusalem. They believe the Shekhinah went into exile with the Jewish people when the Temple was destroyed, and they pray daily for the Temple to be rebuilt and for God's presence to return to Zion, often in the messianic age.

2. Many Reform and Liberal Jews see the Shekhinah as God's closeness felt anywhere: in community, in nature and in ethical action. They do not pray for the Temple sacrifices to be restored, and their prayer books often rephrase those prayers. For them God's presence is found in worship and in working for tikkun olam, not tied to one building.
evidence: Reform siddur revisions of Temple prayers

questions.question: Explain two Jewish teachings about the Shekhinah. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. God's presence dwelt in the Tabernacle and the Temple. God commanded, "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8). When the Tabernacle was completed, a cloud covered it and "the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34). Later the Holy of Holies in Solomon's Temple was understood as the place where God's presence rested, so the Temple became the centre of Jewish worship.

2. The Shekhinah remains with the Jewish people wherever they are. After the destruction of the Temple, the rabbis taught that the Shekhinah went into exile with Israel (Megillah 29a), so God has not abandoned the people. It is present when Jews pray and study together: Pirkei Avot says that when people sit together and discuss Torah, the Shekhinah is among them. This gives comfort in suffering and makes the synagogue a holy place.
questions.examTip: Two developed beliefs or teachings (up to 2 marks each) plus 1 mark for a relevant reference to sacred writings or another source of Jewish teaching, such as the Torah, Tenakh, Talmud or Mishnah. Name the source clearly; it does not have to be word-for-word.

questions.question: Explain two reasons why the Shekhinah is important to Jews. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. It shows that the transcendent God is also close to people. Although God is beyond the universe, the Shekhinah means God dwells among people. Isaiah heard the angels say, "The whole earth is full of his glory" (Isaiah 6:3). This reassures Jews that they can approach God in prayer anywhere, not just in a special place.

2. It comforts Jews through exile and suffering. The rabbis taught that wherever Israel was exiled, the Shekhinah went with them (Megillah 29a). Throughout persecution, including the Holocaust, many Jews have drawn strength from the belief that God shares in their suffering and has not abandoned them. It also gives hope that God's presence will one day be fully restored.

questions.question:
"The Shekhinah can only be experienced in a holy building."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Jewish teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

In the Tenakh, God's presence is closely linked to sacred buildings. God told Moses, "Let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" (Exodus 25:8), and the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle and later Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). The Holy of Holies was so holy that only the High Priest could enter, and only on Yom Kippur. This suggests that God chose to make the Shekhinah dwell in a particular holy place.

Even today, many Jews feel God's presence most strongly in holy places. The synagogue is called a mikdash me'at, a "small sanctuary", which echoes the Temple. The ark containing the Torah scrolls and the ner tamid recall the Temple's holiness. The Western Wall is a place where many feel especially close to God. Orthodox Jews pray for the Temple to be rebuilt so that the Shekhinah may return to Zion, which suggests a link between God's presence and a holy building.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

Jewish teaching says clearly that the Shekhinah is not limited to buildings. The rabbis taught that it rests on any group studying Torah together, even two people (Pirkei Avot 3:2), and that it went into exile with the people after the Temple was destroyed (Megillah 29a). If God's presence were tied to a building, Judaism could not have survived almost two thousand years without the Temple.

The Shekhinah is also found in the home and in ethical action. Shabbat, celebrated mainly at home, is linked with God's presence, and the home is also called a "small sanctuary". The Talmud teaches that God visits the sick, so Jews who visit the sick are following God's ways. Many Reform and Liberal Jews stress that God can be experienced in nature, in community and in working for tikkun olam.

Finally, the Tenakh itself shows God appearing outside buildings: in the burning bush, on Mount Sinai and to the prophet Elijah as "a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12). Isaiah says, "The whole earth is full of his glory."

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

The statement is not convincing. Holy buildings have been, and still are, important places where Jews feel God's presence, but both the Tenakh and rabbinic teaching show that the Shekhinah can be experienced wherever Jews pray, study, keep Shabbat or act with kindness. That Jewish life continued after the Temple's destruction is strong evidence that the Shekhinah is not confined to one place.
questions.examTip: Argue both sides with Jewish teaching, explain why each argument matters (do not just list views), weigh them, and finish with a conclusion that follows from what you have written. Include Orthodox and Reform views where they differ. Spelling, punctuation and grammar are also assessed on 12-mark answers.

questions.question:
"Belief in the Shekhinah is no longer important for Jews because the Temple has been destroyed."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Jewish teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

In the Tenakh, the Shekhinah was most clearly experienced in the Tabernacle and the Temple, as a cloud and as God's glory filling the building. That Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, the sacrifices ended, and nobody has entered the Holy of Holies since. Some would argue that the vivid, visible presence described in Exodus and 1 Kings belongs to the past, and that modern Judaism concentrates instead on keeping the mitzvot and on ethics.

Many Reform and Liberal Jews do not pray for the Temple to be rebuilt and have changed prayers about restoring the Shekhinah to Zion. For some secular or cultural Jews, the idea of God's dwelling presence plays little part in their identity, which centres on family, festivals and community.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

The rabbis taught that the destruction of the Temple did not end the Shekhinah's presence. Instead, the Shekhinah went into exile with the people (Megillah 29a). This belief became more important after 70 CE, not less, because it reassured Jews that God had not abandoned them. Through centuries of persecution, and especially after the Holocaust, many Jews found comfort in the idea that God shares their suffering.

The Shekhinah is now linked with prayer, study and community. Pirkei Avot teaches that when ten people study Torah together, the Shekhinah is present, which helps explain the importance of the minyan and the synagogue as a "small sanctuary". Every weekday Orthodox Jews say in the Amidah, "Blessed are you, Lord, who restores his Shekhinah to Zion," so the belief is part of their daily life.

The belief also shapes ethical life and attitudes to Jerusalem. Jews face Jerusalem to pray, visit the Western Wall, and are taught to imitate God's presence by visiting the sick and comforting mourners. Even Reform Jews who do not want the Temple rebuilt often speak of experiencing God's presence in worship and social action.

JUSTIFIED CONCLUSION

The statement is weak. The destruction of the Temple changed how Jews understand the Shekhinah, but it did not make the belief unimportant; arguably it made it more important, since it moved from a building to the people themselves. Orthodox and Reform Jews interpret it differently, but for both it still explains how God remains close, so the stronger view is that the belief is still significant.
evidence: Amidah blessing for the return to Zion
